title: Turnus certamen poscit
titleEn: Turnus Demands the Duel — Aeneid XII.1–106
about: The last book opens with the Latins beaten twice in the field and every eye turned on Turnus, who had promised to settle the war by meeting Aeneas alone. Like a wounded lion he rouses himself and tells King Latinus to prepare the treaty and the sacrifice: he will kill the Trojan, or Aeneas may have Lavinia. Latinus answers calmly and at length, confessing that he broke the oracle's command to give his daughter to a stranger, and begging Turnus to spare himself and to pity his old father far away in Ardea; his words only make the young man's fever worse. Queen Amata, weeping, implores him not to fight and swears she will not outlive him. Lavinia hears her mother and blushes deeply, the only moment in the poem where we see anything of her feelings, and the sight of her sets Turnus burning the more. He sends a herald to Aeneas with the challenge for the next morning, calls for his horses, puts on his armour and his father's sword, made by Vulcan, and seizes a great spear, praying it will let him drag the effeminate Phrygian's perfumed hair in the dust. The part closes on a simile of a young bull trying his horns before his first fight.

sentences.t:
Turnus ut infractos adverso Marte Latinos
defecisse videt, sua nunc promissa reposci,
se signari oculis, ultro implacabilis ardet
attollitque animos.
sentences.l:
Turnus, when the Latins, broken by hostile Mars,
he sees have given way, his promises now claimed back,
himself marked out by all eyes, unbidden, past appeasing, he burns
and lifts up his spirit.
sentences.i: When Turnus sees the Latins broken by defeat in battle and their spirit failing, sees his promise now called in and every eye fixed on him, he flares up of his own accord, beyond all appeasing, and his pride rises.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough, and the first lines of the last book. 'ut… videt', 'when he sees', 'ut' of time, with three infinitives of indirect statement: the Latins 'defecisse' (have given way), his promises 'reposci' (are being claimed back), he himself 'signari oculis' (is marked out by every eye). 'infractos adverso Marte', 'broken by adverse Mars': Mars stands for battle itself, the defeats of Book XI. 'sua promissa': Turnus had undertaken to meet Aeneas alone (XI.434–444, from memory). 'ultro', 'of his own accord'. 'implacabilis', 'not to be appeased'. 'attollit animos', 'raises his spirits', pride rising to the challenge. Elisions 'signar(i) oculis', 'ultr(o) implacabilis', 'attollitqu(e) animos'.

sentences.t:
Poenorum qualis in arvis
saucius ille gravi venantum vulnere pectus
tum demum movet arma leo gaudetque comantis
excutiens cervice toros fixumque latronis
inpavidus frangit telum et fremit ore cruento:
sentences.l:
As in the fields of the Carthaginians
that lion, wounded by the hunters' heavy wound in the chest,
only then moves his arms, and rejoices, the maned
shaking out on his neck muscles, and the planted spear of the lurking hunter
fearless he breaks and roars with bloody mouth:
sentences.i: As in the fields of Africa a lion, struck in the chest by a grievous wound from the huntsmen, only then rouses himself to fight, exults as he shakes out the thick mane on his neck, snaps unafraid the spear the lurking hunter planted in him, and roars with bloodied jaws:
sentences.n: 'qualis… leo', 'as a lion', the first simile of the book. 'Poenorum… in arvis', 'in the fields of the Carthaginians', Africa, home of lions. 'ille', 'that lion', pointing at the beast as if it stood before us. 'saucius… pectus', 'wounded in the chest', 'pectus' an accusative of respect (the Greek construction). 'tum demum', 'only then', once he is hurt, as Turnus once he is beaten. 'movet arma', 'moves his arms', his claws and teeth. 'comantis… toros', 'maned muscles', the '-is' accusative plural. 'latronis', 'of the man in ambush', an old sense of 'latro', here a hunter lying in wait (L&S). 'inpavidus' is Greenough's spelling of 'impavidus'. Homer compares Achilles to a wounded lion (Iliad XX.164–175, from memory). Elision 'tel(um) et'.

sentences.t: haud secus adcenso gliscit violentia Turno.
sentences.l: not otherwise in the kindled Turnus swells the violence.
sentences.i: Just so the violence swells in Turnus once he is roused.
sentences.n: 'haud secus', 'not otherwise', the formula that closes a simile and turns back to the story. 'adcenso… Turno', 'in Turnus, kindled', most simply a dative of reference; 'adcenso' is Greenough's spelling of 'accenso', keeping the prefix 'ad-' unassimilated. 'gliscit', 'swells, spreads', an old word for something growing unchecked. 'violentia', 'violence', almost a name for Turnus's temper: the word comes back at 45, 'violentia Turni'. No elisions.

sentences.t: Tum sic adfatur regem atque ita turbidus infit:
sentences.l: Then thus he addresses the king and so, stormy, begins:
sentences.i: Then he turns to the king, and in a storm of feeling begins:
sentences.n: 'adfatur', 'addresses', Greenough's spelling of 'affatur', from the deponent 'adfor'. 'regem', Latinus. 'turbidus', 'stormy, troubled', the adjective standing where English would use an adverb (you will see this constantly). 'infit', 'he begins (to speak)', an old defective verb found almost only in this form, a solemn word of epic. 'sic… ita', two words for 'thus', the doubled introduction of a speech. Elision 'reg(em) atque'.

sentences.t:
“Nulla mora in Turno; nihil est quod dicta retractent
ignavi Aeneadae, nec quae pepigere recusent.
sentences.l:
“No delay is in Turnus; there is no reason why their words should take back
the cowardly Aeneadae, nor what they bargained refuse.
sentences.i: “There is no holding back in Turnus; there is no cause for the cowardly Aeneadae to take back their words or go back on what they have agreed.
sentences.n: Turnus's speech opens; it runs to 17. 'Nulla mora (est) in Turno': he names himself in the third person, as a public fact. 'nihil est quod…', 'there is no reason why…', with the subjunctive. 'retractent', 'should withdraw'. 'Aeneadae', 'sons of Aeneas', his men, the patronymic used with contempt beside 'ignavi', 'cowardly'; Ae- is one long syllable. 'pepigere' = 'pepigerunt', 'they agreed', from 'pango', to strike a bargain: Aeneas had offered to settle the war by single combat (XI.115–118, from memory). Elisions 'mor(a) in', 'ignav(i) Aeneadae'.

sentences.t: Congredior, fer sacra, pater, et concipe foedus.
sentences.l: I go to meet him; bring the sacred things, father, and frame the treaty.
sentences.i: I will meet him: bring out the sacred things, father, and draw up the terms of the treaty.
sentences.n: 'Congredior', 'I meet (him)', the present for an immediate future; the verb is used of closing in combat. 'fer sacra', 'bring the sacred things', the victims and implements for the sacrifice that seals a treaty. 'pater', a respectful address to the old king, who is also to be his father-in-law; its short last syllable is lengthened on the beat before the pause. 'concipe foedus', 'frame the treaty', 'concipere' being the word for putting a formula into set words, as in 'concipere verba iuris iurandi'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Aut hac Dardanium dextra sub Tartara mittam,
desertorem Asiae (sedeant spectentque Latini),
et solus ferro crimen commune refellam,
aut habeat victos, cedat Lavinia coniunx.”
sentences.l:
Either with this right hand the Dardanian down to Tartarus I shall send,
the deserter of Asia (let them sit and watch, the Latins),
and alone with the sword the common charge I shall refute,
or let him have us conquered, let Lavinia pass to him as wife.”
sentences.i: Either with this right hand I will send the Dardanian down to Tartarus, that runaway from Asia — let the Latins sit and look on — and with my sword alone refute the charge laid on us all, or let him hold us as his conquered subjects and take Lavinia as his bride.”
sentences.n: 'Aut… aut', 'either… or', the two outcomes. 'hac… dextra', 'with this right hand', with a gesture. 'Dardanium', 'the Dardanian', Aeneas, after Dardanus, founder of Troy's line; 'Tartara', neuter plural of Tartarus, the underworld. 'desertorem Asiae', 'deserter of Asia', a sneer: Aeneas fled when Troy fell. 'sedeant spectentque', jussive subjunctives, like 'habeat' and 'cedat' in 17. 'crimen commune', 'the reproach we share', the charge of cowardice. 'refellam', 'I will refute', from 're-' and 'fallo'. 'cedat… coniunx', 'let her go (to him) as wife'. The speech ends here. Elision 'desertor(em) Asiae'.

sentences.t: Olli sedato respondit corde Latinus:
sentences.l: To him with calmed heart answered Latinus:
sentences.i: Latinus answered him with a quiet heart:
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Olli', the old form of 'illi', 'to him', from archaic 'ollus' for 'ille', kept in epic for its antique colour. 'sedato… corde', 'with a calmed heart', ablative of manner, framing the verb: the old king's composure set against Turnus's storm. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“O praestans animi iuvenis, quantum ipse feroci
virtute exsuperas, tanto me impensius aequum est
consulere atque omnis metuentem expendere casus.
sentences.l:
“O young man outstanding in spirit, as much as you yourself in fierce
valour excel, so much more earnestly it is right for me
to take counsel and, fearing, to weigh all chances.
sentences.i: “Young man of matchless spirit, the further you surpass others in fiery courage, the more it falls to me to take careful thought and, fearful as I am, weigh every hazard.
sentences.n: Latinus's speech opens; it runs to 45. 'praestans animi', 'outstanding in spirit', 'animi' a genitive (or old locative) with an adjective, a poetic construction. 'quantum… tanto', 'by as much as… by so much', correlatives of comparison: the hotter you are, the more careful I must be. 'impensius', 'more earnestly', from 'impensus', costly. 'aequum est', 'it is right'. 'omnis… casus', the '-is' accusative plural, 'all chances'. 'expendere', 'weigh out', a word from the scales. Elisions 'quant(um) ipse', 'virtut(e) exsuperas', 'm(e) impensius', 'aequ(um) est', 'consuler(e) atque', 'atqu(e) omnis', 'metuent(em) expendere'.

sentences.t:
Sunt tibi regna patris Dauni, sunt oppida capta
multa manu, nec non aurumque animusque Latino est;
sentences.l:
You have the realms of your father Daunus, you have towns taken,
many, by your hand; and also both gold and goodwill Latinus has;
sentences.i: You have the kingdom of your father Daunus, you have many towns taken by your own hand; and Latinus, too, has gold and a generous heart;
sentences.n: 'Sunt tibi', 'there are to you', the dative of possession, said twice: 'you have… you have'. Daunus, Turnus's father, king of the Rutulians at Ardea. 'manu', 'by (your) hand', by force. 'nec non', 'and also', two negatives making a strong positive. 'aurumque animusque', double '-que', 'both gold and spirit'; 'animus' is goodwill, readiness to give: Latinus is offering a rich settlement. 'Latino est', dative of possession again, the king speaking of himself by name. Elisions 'aurumqu(e) animusque', 'Latin(o) est'.

sentences.t:
sunt aliae innuptae Latio et Laurentibus arvis,
nec genus indecores.
sentences.l:
there are other unmarried girls in Latium and the Laurentine fields,
not in birth undistinguished.
sentences.i: there are other unwed girls in Latium and the fields of Laurentum, and not of mean birth.
sentences.n: 'sunt aliae innuptae', 'there are other unmarried (girls)': Latinus is offering Turnus another bride. 'Latio et Laurentibus arvis', ablatives of place without a preposition. 'nec genus indecores', 'and not without distinction as to birth': 'genus' is an accusative of respect (the Greek construction), and 'indecores' comes from the rarer third-declension adjective 'indecoris', as 'indecorem' at XI.845. Elisions 'ali(ae) innuptae', 'Lati(o) et'.

sentences.t:
Sine me haec haud mollia fatu
sublatis aperire dolis, simul hoc animo hauri.
sentences.l:
Allow me these things, not soft to speak,
with wiles put away to lay open; at the same time drink this in with your mind.
sentences.i: Let me lay bare these things, hard as they are to say, with all pretence set aside; and take this deep into your mind as well.
sentences.n: 'Sine me… aperire', 'allow me to disclose', 'sine' the imperative of 'sino', not the preposition. 'haud mollia fatu', 'not soft to speak', 'fatu' the supine in '-u' of 'for', saying in what respect: hard words. 'sublatis… dolis', ablative absolute, 'with deceits removed', without concealment. 'simul', 'at the same time', 'and with it'. 'animo hauri', 'drain this with your mind', take it in to the bottom, a metaphor from drinking. Elisions 'm(e) haec', 'anim(o) hauri'.

sentences.t:
Me natam nulli veterum sociare procorum
fas erat, idque omnes divique hominesque canebant.
sentences.l:
For me my daughter to none of her old suitors to join
was lawful, and this all, both gods and men, were foretelling.
sentences.i: Heaven's law did not allow me to give my daughter to any of her former suitors, and all, gods and men alike, foretold as much.
sentences.n: 'Me… sociare… fas erat', 'it was right for me to join', the infinitive with subject accusative 'me' after 'fas erat', 'it was allowed by divine law'; the negative lies in 'nulli', 'to none'. 'veterum… procorum', 'of the old suitors', the Italian princes, Turnus among them, who sought Lavinia before the Trojans came. 'canebant', 'kept chanting', 'cano' of prophecy: the oracle of Faunus had told Latinus to wed her to a stranger from abroad (VII.96–101, from memory). 'divique hominesque', double '-que'. Elisions 'idqu(e) omnes', 'diviqu(e) hominesque'.

sentences.t:
Victus amore tui, cognato sanguine victus
coniugis et maestae lacrumis, vincla omnia rupi:
sentences.l:
Overcome by love of you, by kindred blood overcome
and by my sorrowing wife's tears, the bonds all I broke:
sentences.i: Won over by my affection for you, won over by the blood we share and by my grieving wife's tears, I broke every bond:
sentences.n: 'Victus… victus', 'overcome… overcome', the word framing the line, repeated by a man explaining his weakness. 'amore tui', 'by love of you', the objective genitive of the pronoun. 'cognato sanguine', 'by kindred blood': Turnus is kin to Amata, Latinus's queen (by tradition her sister's son, from memory). 'coniugis… maestae lacrumis', 'by the tears of my sad wife'; 'lacrumis' is Greenough's old spelling of 'lacrimis'. 'vincla', syncopated 'vincula', the bonds of oracle and promise. Elision 'vincl(a) omnia'.

sentences.t: promissam eripui genero, arma impia sumpsi.
sentences.l: the promised girl I snatched from my son-in-law, arms unholy I took up.
sentences.i: I tore the promised bride from my son-in-law and took up an impious war.
sentences.n: 'promissam', 'the (girl) promised', Lavinia, pledged to Aeneas in Book VII. 'genero', 'from my son-in-law', a dative of separation with 'eripui': Latinus already calls Aeneas son-in-law. 'arma impia', 'impious arms': a war against an oracle and a promise is a sin. Two short clauses without a connective (asyndeton), the rhythm of a confession. Elisions 'promiss(am) eripui', 'arm(a) impia'; but 'genero, arma' does not elide: the long '-o' stands before the pause in hiatus, one of Virgil's rare unelided meetings of vowels.

sentences.t:
Ex illo qui me casus, quae, Turne, sequantur
bella, vides, quantos primus patiare labores.
sentences.l:
Since then what misfortunes me, what, Turnus, pursue,
what wars, you see, how great the toils you first endure.
sentences.i: Since then, Turnus, you see what misfortunes, what wars hound me, and what heavy trials you yourself are the first to bear.
sentences.n: 'Ex illo (tempore)', 'from that time'. 'qui… casus, quae… bella… sequantur', indirect questions after 'vides', with the subjunctive; 'quantos… patiare… labores' is a third. 'patiare' = 'patiaris', the alternative second-singular ending in '-re' (you will meet it often). 'primus', 'first, foremost': the leader takes the brunt. 'Turne', vocative, set inside the clause. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Bis magna victi pugna vix urbe tuemur
spes Italas;
sentences.l:
Twice in a great battle beaten, barely within the city we guard
the hopes of Italy;
sentences.i: Twice beaten in a great battle, we can barely guard the hopes of Italy behind our walls;
sentences.n: 'Bis… victi', 'twice beaten', in the battles of Books X and XI. 'magna… pugna', ablative of means, its words parted by 'victi'. 'urbe', 'in the city', ablative of place: the Latins are reduced to defending their walls. 'tuemur', 'we guard', a deponent. 'spes Italas', 'the hopes of Italy', the whole Italian cause. No elisions.

sentences.t:
recalent nostro Thybrina fluenta
sanguine adhuc campique ingentes ossibus albent.
sentences.l:
warm again with our are the Tiber's streams
blood still, and the plains, vast, with bones grow white.
sentences.i: the waters of the Tiber are still warm with our blood, and the wide plains are white with bones.
sentences.n: 'recalent', 'are warm again', still warm, the 're-' marking a state that persists. 'Thybrina fluenta', 'the Thybrine streams', the Tiber under its poetic name 'Thybris'. 'nostro… sanguine', ablative of cause, split across the line-end. 'campique ingentes', 'and the vast plains'. 'albent', 'are white', with the bones of the unburied, an exaggeration of how long the war has lasted. Elisions 'sanguin(e) adhuc', 'campiqu(e) ingentes'.

sentences.t: Quo referor totiens?
sentences.l: Where am I carried back so often?
sentences.i: Why do I keep drifting back?
sentences.n: Latinus breaks off and turns on himself. 'Quo referor', 'where am I being carried back', a passive with the sense of being swept back, like a ship, to the old position. 'totiens', 'so many times': he has changed his mind again and again. A short self-reproaching question, the first of a series. No elisions.

sentences.t: Quae mentem insania mutat?
sentences.l: What madness changes my mind?
sentences.i: What madness keeps turning my judgement?
sentences.n: 'insania', 'madness', a hard word for his own wavering against the plain command of the oracle. 'mentem… mutat', 'changes my mind', a present of something that keeps happening: each time, the queen's tears and his own fondness undo his judgement. Elision 'ment(em) insania'.

sentences.t:
Si Turno exstincto socios sum adscire paratus,
cur non incolumi potius certamina tollo?
sentences.l:
If, Turnus slain, as allies I am ready to take them,
why not, with him unharmed, rather do I end the contests?
sentences.i: If I am prepared to take the Trojans as allies once Turnus is dead, why not end the fighting instead while he is still unharmed?
sentences.n: 'Turno exstincto', ablative absolute, 'Turnus being destroyed'; 'incolumi' (with 'Turno' understood), 'him being safe', a second ablative absolute set against the first. 'socios… adscire', 'to take on (the Trojans) as allies', 'socios' a predicate; 'adscire' is Greenough's spelling of 'ascire', 'to admit, adopt'. 'certamina tollo', 'do I remove the contest'. The logic is plain: a peace after his death is pointless when a peace before it would save him. Elisions 'Turn(o) exstincto', 's(um) adscire'.

sentences.t:
Quid consanguinei Rutuli, quid cetera dicet
Italia, ad mortem si te—Fors dicta refutet!—
prodiderim, natam et conubia nostra petentem?
sentences.l:
What will the Rutulians, my blood-kin, what will the rest of
Italy say, if you to death — may Chance unsay the words! —
I should betray, you who seek my daughter and marriage with us?
sentences.i: What will the Rutulians, my own kin, say, what will the rest of Italy say, if I betray you to death — may Chance prove the words false! — when you are seeking my daughter's hand and a marriage with my house?
sentences.n: 'consanguinei', 'of the same blood', the Rutulians as Latinus's kin, through Turnus's tie to Amata or simply as a kindred people of Latium; one verb, 'dicet', serves both subjects. 'cetera… Italia', 'the rest of Italy', split across the line. 'si… prodiderim', 'if I should betray', perfect subjunctive in a future condition, seeing the deed as already done. 'Fors dicta refutet!', 'may Chance refute my words!', a wish thrown in between dashes to ward off the ill omen of saying 'death'. 'natam et conubia nostra petentem', 'seeking my daughter and marriage with us', the participle agreeing with 'te'; 'conubia', 'marriage(-rights)'. Elisions 'Itali(a) ad', 'nat(am) et'.

sentences.t:
Respice res bello varias; miserere parentis
longaevi, quem nunc maestum patria Ardea longe
dividit.
sentences.l:
Consider the fortunes of war, how they change; pity your father,
aged, whom now, sorrowing, his homeland Ardea far away
keeps apart.”
sentences.i: Consider how fortune shifts in war; have pity on your aged father, whom his homeland Ardea now keeps far from you and grieving.”
sentences.n: The print has 'dividit. ”Haudquaquam', a misprint for 'dividit.” Haudquaquam', corrected here. The mark closing Latinus's speech is set after a space and joined to the next word, as at XI.849, so t keeps the print and the mark stands at the head of the next unit, while l and i close the speech after 'dividit.'. 'Respice', 'look back on, consider'. 'res bello varias', 'affairs changeable in war'. 'miserere', imperative of the deponent 'misereor', with the genitive 'parentis'. 'longaevi', 'long-lived, aged', Daunus. 'patria Ardea', his native town, the Rutulian capital. Elision 'patri(a) Ardea'.

sentences.t:
”Haudquaquam dictis violentia Turni
flectitur:
sentences.l:
By no means by the words the violence of Turnus
is bent:
sentences.i: Words do nothing at all to bend Turnus's violence:
sentences.n: The print has 'dividit. ”Haudquaquam', a misprint for 'dividit.” Haudquaquam', corrected here; the mark at the head of t belongs to the speech just ended, so l and i carry none. 'Haudquaquam', 'by no means', a strong negative. 'dictis', ablative of means, Latinus's words. 'violentia Turni', the word of line 9 again, almost a character in its own right. 'flectitur', 'is bent', the image of trying to turn something rigid. No elisions.

sentences.t: exsuperat magis aegrescitque medendo.
sentences.l: it rises the more and sickens with the healing.
sentences.i: it only surges further, and every attempt to treat it makes the sickness worse.
sentences.n: 'exsuperat', 'surges over', a word used of flames or a flood rising above a barrier. 'aegrescit… medendo', 'grows sick through healing', 'medendo' a gerund in the ablative, 'by the treating': the doctor's attempt makes the patient worse. The medical metaphor makes Turnus's rage a disease, and the paradox is compact enough to be quoted on its own. No elisions.

sentences.t: Ut primum fari potuit, sic institit ore:
sentences.l: As soon as to speak he was able, thus he began with his lips:
sentences.i: As soon as he could find his voice, he began:
sentences.n: 'Ut primum', 'as soon as', with the perfect. 'fari potuit', 'he was able to speak': rage at first chokes him. 'institit', 'set about (speaking)', from 'insisto', to press on with something. 'ore', 'with his mouth', making the speaking physical, a fuller version of the usual formula of address. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Quam pro me curam geris, hanc precor, optime, pro me
deponas letumque sinas pro laude pacisci:
sentences.l:
“The care which for me you bear, this, I pray, best of men, for me
lay aside, and allow me death for glory to bargain:
sentences.i: “The concern you feel for me, best of men, I beg you, put it aside for my sake, and let me trade my death for glory:
sentences.n: Turnus's reply opens; it runs to 53. 'Quam… curam… hanc', 'what care… this (care)', the relative clause put first and picked up by the demonstrative. 'pro me… pro me', 'for me… for my sake', the same words with a new turn. 'precor… deponas', 'I pray you lay aside', the subjunctive without 'ut' after a verb of asking. 'optime', 'best (of men)', a courteous vocative. 'letum… pro laude pacisci', 'to bargain death for glory', 'pacisci' a deponent, 'to make a bargain': the heroic exchange chosen by Achilles. No elisions.

sentences.t:
et nos tela, pater, ferrumque haud debile dextra
spargimus;
sentences.l:
We too weapons, father, and steel not feeble with our right hand
scatter;
sentences.i: I too, father, can hurl spears and steel with no feeble hand;
sentences.n: 'et nos', 'we too': 'nos' is Turnus himself, the poetic plural, and 'et' means 'also', as well as Aeneas. 'tela… ferrumque', 'missiles and steel'. 'haud debile', 'not feeble', understatement (litotes) for 'strong'. 'dextra', 'with the right hand', ablative of instrument. 'spargimus', 'we scatter', throw broadcast. Elision 'ferrumqu(e) haud'.

sentences.t: et nostro sequitur de volnere sanguis.
sentences.l: and from our wound follows blood.
sentences.i: and the wounds I give draw blood as well.
sentences.n: 'nostro… de volnere', 'from a wound of ours', one we give, not one we take; 'volnere' is Greenough's old spelling of 'vulnere'. 'sequitur', 'follows', the blood coming after the blow. Aeneas is not the only one whose spear does harm: Turnus answers Latinus's fear for him with a boast. No elisions.

sentences.t:
longe illi dea mater erit, quae nube fugacem
feminea tegat et vanis sese occulat umbris.”
sentences.l:
Far away for him his goddess mother will be, to cover the runaway in a cloud
womanish and hide herself in empty shadows.”
sentences.i: His goddess mother will be far from him, with no woman's cloud to shield her runaway and no empty shadows for her to hide in.”
sentences.n: The print has lower-case 'longe' after the full stop ending 51, a misprint for 'Longe', corrected here. 'longe… erit', 'will be far off'; 'illi', 'for him', Aeneas. 'dea mater', Venus. 'quae… tegat… occulat', a relative clause of purpose, 'to hide': there will be no goddess at hand to do it. In the Iliad Aphrodite carries Aeneas away from Diomedes in her robe and Apollo then hides him in a dark cloud (V.311–345, from memory). 'nube… feminea', 'a womanish cloud', a sneer at a man saved by his mother. 'fugacem', 'the runaway'. 'sese', grammatically the goddess herself. The speech ends here. Elisions 'long(e) illi', 'ses(e) occulat'.

sentences.t:
At regina, nova pugnae conterrita sorte,
flebat et ardentem generum monitura tenebat:
sentences.l:
But the queen, by the new turn of the fight terrified,
was weeping, and her fiery son-in-law, meaning to counsel him, was holding:
sentences.i: But the queen, terrified at this new turn in the contest, was weeping, and clung to her fiery son-in-law, intent on counselling him:
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'regina', Amata, Latinus's queen and Turnus's champion since Book VII. 'nova pugnae… sorte', 'by the new lot of the fight', the single combat now agreed. 'generum', 'son-in-law', as she still calls Turnus. 'monitura', future participle of 'moneo', 'meaning to warn': Greenough's reading. The Latin Library has 'moritura', 'resolved to die', which turns her whole speech into the plea of a woman set on death (she says she will not outlive him, 62–63) and looks ahead to her end in this book; both construe, and the sense differs. 'flebat… tenebat', imperfects, a scene held still. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Turne, per has ego te lacrimas, per siquis Amatae
tangit honos animum (spes tu nunc una, senectae
tu requies miserae, decus imperiumque Latini
te penes, in te omnis domus inclinata recumbit).
unum oro:
sentences.l:
“Turnus, by these, I beg you, tears, by whatever regard for Amata
touches your heart (you are now my one hope, of my old age
you are the rest, wretched as it is; the glory and the power of Latinus
lie with you, on you the whole house leans and rests),
one thing I beg:
sentences.i: “Turnus, by these tears, by whatever regard for Amata touches your heart — you are my one hope now, the comfort of my unhappy age, the honour and the sovereignty of Latinus are in your keeping, the whole house leans its weight on you — one thing I beg of you:
sentences.n: The print has 'recumbit).' with a full stop, then lower-case 'unum', a misprint for a comma, corrected here: the oath 'per has… lacrimas, per… honos' needs its verb and finds it in 'oro'. t keeps the print and the unit runs on across the stop. Amata's speech opens; it runs to 63. 'per has ego te lacrimas', 'by these tears I (beg) you', the pronouns set between 'per' and its noun, the word order of entreaty. 'siquis… honos', 'if any regard'. 'senectae… miserae', 'of my unhappy old age'. 'te penes', 'in your keeping', 'penes' after its pronoun. 'inclinata recumbit', 'leans and rests', a falling house on its one prop. Elisions 'in t(e) omnis', 'un(um) oro'.

sentences.t: desiste manum committere Teucris.
sentences.l: cease to engage your hand in combat with the Teucrians.
sentences.i: give up meeting the Trojans hand to hand.
sentences.n: 'desiste', 'stop, desist', with the infinitive. 'manum committere', 'to join hand (in battle)', the idiom of 'manum' or 'proelium committere', to engage. 'Teucris', dative, 'with the Teucrians', the Trojans, named after their ancestor Teucer; 'eu' is one syllable. The whole of Amata's speech hangs on this one plea. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Qui te cumque manent isto certamine casus,
et me, Turne, manent:
sentences.l:
Whatever misfortunes await you in that contest of yours,
me too, Turnus, they await:
sentences.i: Whatever fate awaits you in that contest awaits me too, Turnus:
sentences.n: 'Qui… cumque', 'whatever', 'quicumque' split by 'te' (tmesis, a word cut in two). 'manent', 'await', with an accusative of the person. 'isto certamine', 'in that contest of yours', 'iste' with a note of distaste. 'et me', 'me also'. The repeated verb ties her fate to his. No elisions.

sentences.t:
simul haec invisa relinquam
lumina nec generum Aenean captiva videbo.”
sentences.l:
at once this hateful I shall leave
light, and not Aeneas as son-in-law, a captive, shall I see.”
sentences.i: I will leave this light I have come to hate at the same moment as you, and I will not live on as a captive to see Aeneas become my son-in-law.”
sentences.n: 'simul', 'together, at the same moment', with you. 'haec… lumina', 'this light', the daylight of life, and 'invisa', 'hateful': she means to die. 'generum Aenean', 'Aeneas as son-in-law', 'generum' a predicate; 'Aenean' is a Greek accusative, its Ae- one long syllable. 'captiva', 'a captive', what she would be in a Trojan victory. The words look ahead to her death later in this book. The speech ends here. Elision 'gener(um) Aenean'.

sentences.t:
Accepit vocem lacrimis Lavinia matris
flagrantis perfusa genas, quoi plurimus ignem
subiecit rubor et calefacta per ora cucurrit.
sentences.l:
Lavinia took in her mother's words, with tears
her burning cheeks drenched, in whom a deep fire
a blush kindled beneath, and over her heated face it ran.
sentences.i: Lavinia heard her mother's words, her burning cheeks bathed in tears, while a deep blush lit a fire in her and spread over her glowing face.
sentences.n: 'Accepit vocem… matris', 'took in her mother's voice', heard her. 'lacrimis… perfusa genas', 'drenched as to her cheeks with tears', 'genas' an accusative of respect (the Greek construction, common with passive participles); 'flagrantis', '-is' accusative plural with 'genas', 'burning'. 'quoi' is Greenough's old spelling of 'cui', one long syllable, 'to whom', a dative of reference: 'in whom'. 'plurimus… rubor', 'a deep blush', which 'ignem subiecit', 'set fire beneath', like fuel kindled under a pot. Virgil does not say why she blushes. This is the one moment in the poem where Lavinia shows any feeling, and she never speaks. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Indum sanguineo veluti violaverit ostro
siquis ebur, aut mixta rubent ubi lilia multa
alba rosa:
sentences.l:
As if Indian with blood-red should stain purple
someone ivory, or as when, mingled, lilies blush, white,
with much rose:
sentences.i: As when someone stains Indian ivory with blood-red purple, or as white lilies glow red when many roses are mingled with them:
sentences.n: 'veluti… siquis… violaverit', 'as if someone should stain', the perfect subjunctive in a simile of supposed action. 'Indum… ebur', 'Indian ivory', framing the clause; 'ostro', 'with purple dye', the costly sea-purple; 'violaverit', 'has stained', but also 'has violated', a hint of hurt inside the picture of beauty. Homer compares blood on Menelaus's thigh to a woman staining ivory with purple (Iliad IV.141–147, from memory). 'mixta… multa… rosa', 'mingled with much rose', the ablative 'multa… rosa' parted from 'mixta'; 'alba' agrees with 'lilia'. 'ebur' has its short last syllable lengthened on the beat before the pause. No elisions.

sentences.t: talis virgo dabat ore colores.
sentences.l: such colours the maiden was giving in her face.
sentences.i: such were the colours the maiden's face showed.
sentences.n: 'talis… colores', 'such colours', framing the clause and closing the simile. 'virgo', Lavinia. 'dabat ore', 'was giving in her face', showed; 'ore' is an ablative of place, 'os' the face. Red on white was the ancient picture of a beautiful complexion, and the blush is all we are told of what she feels. No elisions.

sentences.t: Illum turbat amor, figitque in virgine voltus:
sentences.l: Him love throws into turmoil, and he fixes on the maiden his looks:
sentences.i: Love throws Turnus into turmoil, and he fastens his eyes on the girl:
sentences.n: 'Illum', Turnus, put first. 'turbat amor', 'love unsettles (him)', the only place in the poem where Turnus is said to love Lavinia. 'figit… voltus', 'fixes his looks', 'voltus' Greenough's old spelling of 'vultus', plural for the face or gaze. 'in virgine', 'on the maiden'. Elision 'figitqu(e) in'.

sentences.t: ardet in arma magis paucisque adfatur Amatam.
sentences.l: he burns for arms the more, and in few words addresses Amata.
sentences.i: He burns all the more for the fight, and speaks a few words to Amata.
sentences.n: 'ardet in arma', 'burns towards arms', 'in' of purpose, eager for battle. 'magis', 'the more': the sight of her sharpens his resolve. 'paucis (verbis)', 'in a few words'. 'adfatur', 'addresses', Greenough's spelling of 'affatur', as at 10. Elision 'paucisqu(e) adfatur'.

sentences.i: “Do not, I beg you, mother, do not send me off with tears and so dark an omen as I go into the trials of cruel war;
sentences.n: Turnus's reply opens; it runs to 80. 'Ne… prosequere', 'do not escort', 'ne' with the present imperative of the deponent, a poetic and old-fashioned prohibition. 'neve', 'or not'. 'omine tanto', 'with so great an omen': tears at a parting were thought to bring bad luck. 'duri certamina Martis', 'the contests of hard Mars', war. 'euntem', 'going', agrees with 'me'. 'O mater': he addresses his future mother-in-law as mother. Elisions 'nev(e) omine', 'prosequer(e) in'.

sentences.t: neque enim Turno mora libera mortis.
sentences.l: for not to Turnus is the delaying of death free.
sentences.i: for it is not in Turnus's power to put off his death.
sentences.n: 'neque enim', 'for… not'. 'Turno… mora libera mortis', 'to Turnus (there is) no free delay of death', dative of possession: whether his death comes now or later is not his to choose, and if it is fated, tears will not hold it back. 'mortis', objective genitive with 'mora'. The thought is Hector's to Andromache, that no man dies before his destined day (Iliad VI.487–489, from memory). Elision 'nequ(e) enim'.

sentences.t:
Nuntius haec Idmon Phrygio mea dicta tyranno
haud placitura refer:
sentences.l:
As messenger these, Idmon, to the Phrygian tyrant, my words,
not going to please, carry back:
sentences.i: Idmon, be my messenger and carry these words of mine to the Phrygian tyrant, words he will not like:
sentences.n: 'Idmon', a herald, named only here; 'nuntius', 'as messenger', in apposition. 'Phrygio… tyranno', 'to the Phrygian tyrant', Aeneas: 'Phrygian' is contemptuous, the soft Asiatic, and 'tyrannus', a Greek word for a ruler, can mean simply 'king' but here carries its sting. 'haec… mea dicta… haud placitura', 'these words of mine, not going to please', the future participle. 'refer', 'carry back'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
cum primum crastina caelo
puniceis invecta rotis Aurora rubebit,
non Teucros agat in Rutulos, Teucrum arma quiescant
et Rutuli;
sentences.i: as soon as tomorrow's Dawn, borne on her crimson wheels, reddens in the sky, let him not lead Trojans against Rutulians; let the Trojans' arms be still, and the Rutulians too;
sentences.n: 'cum primum', 'as soon as', with a future. 'crastina… Aurora', 'tomorrow's Dawn', the goddess driving her chariot ('rotis', 'wheels') into the sky; 'puniceis', 'crimson', a word related to 'Poenus', Phoenician, from the Tyrian dye. 'non… agat', 'let him not lead', jussive with 'non' for the usual 'ne'. 'Teucrum' = 'Teucrorum', the old genitive plural; 'eu' is one syllable in 'Teucros' and 'Teucrum'. 'et Rutuli', 'and (let) the Rutulians (rest)', a second subject added loosely. Elision 'Teucr(um) arma'.

sentences.t:
nostro dirimamus sanguine bellum,
illo quaeratur coniunx Lavinia campo.”
sentences.l:
with our let us settle blood the war;
on that let be sought as wife Lavinia field.”
sentences.i: let us decide the war with our own blood; on that field let Lavinia be won as a bride.”
sentences.n: 'dirimamus', 'let us decide', jussive; 'dirimo' is literally 'part, separate', the word for breaking up a fight. 'nostro… sanguine', 'with our blood', his and Aeneas's: the plural takes in both champions. 'illo… campo', 'on that field', framing the line, ablative of place. 'quaeratur', 'let her be sought', won. 'coniunx', 'as wife', a predicate. The speech ends here. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi dicta dedit rapidusque in tecta recessit.
poscit equos gaudetque tuens ante ora frementis,
Pilumno quos ipsa decus dedit Orithyia,
qui candore nives anteirent, cursibus auras.
sentences.l:
These words when he had spoken and swiftly into the palace withdrawn,
he calls for his horses and rejoices, watching before his face them snorting,
which to Pilumnus as a glory Orithyia herself gave,
which in whiteness would outdo snows, in running the winds.
sentences.i: When he has said this and hurried back into the palace, he calls for his horses and delights to watch them snorting before his eyes, the team that Orithyia herself gave Pilumnus as a mark of honour, such as to outdo the snow in whiteness and the winds in speed.
sentences.n: The print has 'recessit.' with a full stop, then lower-case 'poscit', a misprint for a comma, corrected here: 'ubi… dedit… recessit' is a clause of time whose main verb is 'poscit'. t keeps the print and the unit runs on across the stop. A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Haec ubi dicta dedit', the formula that ends a speech. 'frementis', '-is' accusative plural, 'snorting'. 'Pilumno', Pilumnus, an old Italian god, Turnus's grandfather (X.76). 'Orithyia', the Athenian princess carried off by Boreas, the North Wind: horses bred of the wind. The name is four syllables, Ō-rī-thyi-a, and makes the fifth foot a spondee, a heavy Greek close. 'decus', 'as a glory', in apposition. 'qui… anteirent', a relative clause of characteristic, 'such as to outstrip'; 'antei-' is run together as two syllables. Elisions 'rapidusqu(e) in', 'ant(e) ora'.

sentences.t:
Circumstant properi aurigae manibusque lacessunt
pectora plausa cavis et colla comantia pectunt.
sentences.l:
Around them stand the busy grooms, and with hands they rouse
the chests, patted with hollow palms, and the maned necks comb.
sentences.i: The grooms stand round in haste, rousing the horses with the slap of cupped hands on their chests and combing their flowing manes.
sentences.n: 'properi', 'hurrying', an adjective with adverbial force. 'aurigae', 'charioteers', here the grooms who tend the team. 'manibus… cavis', 'with hollow hands', cupped palms that make a ringing slap, the adjective parted from its noun across the line. 'lacessunt pectora plausa', 'they excite the chests, patted', i.e. they rouse them by patting: the participle tells how. 'colla comantia', 'maned necks'; 'pectunt', 'they comb', a sound-play on 'pectora'. Elision 'proper(i) aurigae'.

sentences.t:
Ipse dehinc auro squalentem alboque orichalco
circumdat loricam umeris;
sentences.l:
He himself then, with gold rough and with white orichalc,
puts the breastplate around his shoulders;
sentences.i: Next Turnus himself puts on his shoulders a breastplate rough with gold and white orichalc;
sentences.n: 'Ipse', Turnus himself, after the grooms. 'dehinc', 'next', here two syllables (it is often run together into one). 'squalentem', 'rough, scaly', thick with ornament, like a snake's scales. 'orichalco', 'orichalc', a precious pale alloy, in Greek 'mountain-copper', which Latin also spelt 'aurichalcum' as if 'gold-copper'; 'albo', 'white', its pale sheen. 'circumdat… umeris', 'puts around his shoulders', with the dative; 'umeris', also spelled 'humeris'. Elisions 'squalent(em) alboque', 'alboqu(e) orichalco', 'loric(am) umeris'.

sentences.t:
simul aptat habendo
ensemque clipeumque et rubrae cornua cristae.
ensem, quem Dauno ignipotens deus ipse parenti
fecerat et Stygia candentem tinxerat unda.
sentences.l:
at the same time he fits for holding
both the sword and the shield and the horns of the red crest,
the sword which for Daunus, his father, the fire-lord god himself
had made, and glowing in Stygian water had dipped.
sentences.i: At the same time he fits himself with sword and shield and the horns of his crimson crest — the sword that the fire-lord god himself had made for his father Daunus and plunged glowing into the waters of the Styx.
sentences.n: The print has 'cristae.' with a full stop, then lower-case 'ensem', a misprint for a comma, corrected here: 'ensem' in 90 takes up 'ensemque' and begins the sword's history. t keeps the print and the unit runs on across the stop. 'aptat habendo', 'fits for holding', the dative of the gerund for purpose: he makes them ready to his grip. 'ensemque clipeumque', double '-que', the first '-que' lengthened on the beat, a Homeric licence. 'cornua cristae', the horns that held the plume of his helmet. 'ignipotens', 'lord of fire', Vulcan, who also made Aeneas's arms in Book VIII. 'Stygia… unda', 'in Stygian water', the quenching that tempers steel, given an infernal touch. Elisions 'clipeumqu(e) et', 'Daun(o) ignipotens'.

sentences.t:
Exin quae mediis ingenti adnixa columnae
aedibus adstabat, validam vi corripit hastam,
Actoris Aurunci spolium, quassatque trementem
vociferans:
sentences.l:
Next, which in the middle against a huge column leaning
of the hall stood, the strong spear with force he seizes,
the spoil of Actor the Auruncan, and shakes it, quivering,
shouting:
sentences.i: Then he wrenches up the strong spear that stood propped against a huge column in the middle of the hall, spoil taken from Actor the Auruncan, and shakes it till it quivers, shouting:
sentences.n: 'Exin', 'next', Greenough's form of 'exinde' (the Latin Library prints 'exim'). The relative clause 'quae… adstabat' comes before its noun, 'hastam', so the spear is described before it is named. 'mediis… aedibus', 'in the middle of the house', split across the line-end. 'adnixa', 'leaning against', with the dative 'columnae'; 'adstabat' is Greenough's spelling of 'astabat'. 'validam vi', strength set against strength. 'Actoris Aurunci spolium', 'spoil of Actor the Auruncan', in apposition, a spear taken from a beaten enemy; the Aurunci were an old people of Campania. 'trementem', 'quivering', the result of the shaking. Elision 'ingent(i) adnixa'.

sentences.t:
“Nunc, O numquam frustrata vocatus
hasta meos, nunc tempus adest: te maximus Actor
te Turni nunc dextra gerit.
sentences.l:
“Now, O never having cheated the summons,
spear, of mine, now the time is here: you mighty Actor,
you now Turnus's right hand carries.
sentences.i: “Now, spear, you that never failed me when I called on you, now the hour has come: once great Actor carried you, now Turnus's hand bears you.
sentences.n: Turnus's address to his spear opens; it runs to 100. 'O numquam frustrata vocatus… meos', 'O you who never cheated my calls', 'frustrata' a deponent participle with active sense, 'vocatus' the accusative plural of the fourth-declension noun 'vocatus', 'summons'. 'nunc… nunc… nunc', the triple 'now' of a man who cannot wait. 'te… te', the repeated pronoun: a weapon passes from one great owner to another. 'gerit', 'bears', with 'gerebat' to be supplied for Actor. A speech to a weapon is rare in epic; Achilles speaks to his horses in Homer (Iliad XIX.400–403, from memory). No elisions.

sentences.t:
Da sternere corpus
loricamque manu valida lacerare revulsam
semiviri Phrygis et foedare in pulvere crinis
vibratos calido ferro murraque madentis.”
sentences.l:
Grant me to lay low the body
and the breastplate with strong hand to tear, wrenched off,
of the half-man Phrygian, and to befoul in the dust his locks,
curled with the hot iron and with myrrh dripping.”
sentences.i: Grant that I may bring down the body of that Phrygian half-man, rip his breastplate from him and tear it apart with a strong hand, and to foul in the dust his hair, crimped with hot irons and dripping with myrrh.”
sentences.n: 'Da', 'grant', with three infinitives, 'sternere… lacerare… foedare'. 'loricamque… revulsam', 'and the breastplate torn away', the participle telling what is done first. 'semiviri Phrygis', 'of the half-man Phrygian', the old Italian sneer at Trojan softness (Iarbas uses 'semivir' of Aeneas's company in Book IV, from memory). 'crinis', '-is' accusative plural, 'hair'. 'vibratos calido ferro', 'curled with the hot iron', curling tongs; 'murra', myrrh, a perfumed oil: Turnus jeers at a dandy. The speech ends here. Elision 'foedar(e) in'.

sentences.t: His agitur furiis;
sentences.l: By these he is driven, furies;
sentences.i: Such is the frenzy that drives him;
sentences.n: 'His… furiis', 'by these furies', ablative of cause: the Furies were the goddesses of madness and vengeance, and 'furiae' is also simply 'frenzy'. 'agitur', 'is driven', like an animal under the goad. A short clause that sums up the speech before the picture of his blazing face. No elisions.

sentences.t:
totoque ardentis ab ore
scintillae absistunt, oculis micat acribus ignis:
sentences.l:
and from the whole face of him burning
sparks leap away, in his keen eyes flashes fire:
sentences.i: sparks fly from all his blazing face, and fire flashes from his fierce eyes:
sentences.n: 'toto… ab ore', 'from his whole face', framing the clause; 'ardentis', genitive, 'of him blazing'. 'scintillae absistunt', 'sparks stand off, fly away', an unusual use of 'absisto'. 'oculis… acribus', 'in his keen eyes', ablative of place. Virgil makes the metaphor of fiery rage literal, as Homer does with the flame that blazes from Achilles' head (Iliad XVIII.205–214, from memory). Elisions 'totoqu(e) ardentis', 'scintill(ae) absistunt'.

sentences.t:
mugitus veluti cum prima in proelia taurus
terrificos ciet atque irasci in cornua temptat,
arboris obnixus trunco, ventosque lacessit
ictibus aut sparsa ad pugnam proludit harena.
sentences.l:
bellowings as when before his first battles a bull
terrifying raises and to put his anger into his horns tries,
against a tree's trunk thrusting, and the winds provokes
with blows, or with sand scattered for the fight rehearses.
sentences.i: just as a bull before his first battle raises terrible bellowings and tries to gather his anger into his horns, butting against a tree-trunk and striking at the winds, or tosses up the sand in a prelude to the fight.
sentences.n: 'veluti cum', 'as when', a simile Virgil had drawn already in Georgics III, of a bull training for battle (from memory). 'mugitus… terrificos', 'terrifying bellowings', parted across the line-end. 'ciet', 'stirs up, raises'. 'irasci in cornua', 'to put his anger into his horns', to gather his rage into them. 'obnixus', 'pressing against', with the dative 'trunco'. 'ventos lacessit ictibus', 'provokes the winds with blows', thrusts at empty air. 'proludit', 'practises beforehand', a gladiator's word. The Latin Library reads 'aut' for 'atque' in 104, making the bellowing and the trial of the horns alternatives; the sense hardly changes. Elisions 'prim(a) in', 'atqu(e) irasci', 'irasc(i) in', 'spars(a) ad'.
